title: The Great Zombification
author: Owen Yingling
summary: A 21-year-old UChicago student-writer documents the metastatic spread of AI use on elite campuses, arguing it has moved from academic misconduct into wholesale substitution of machine output for the human acts that constitute genuine education: learning, teaching, and conversing. Drawing on vivid firsthand accounts—students photographing exams to send to ChatGPT, The Maroon publishing AI-generated articles, professors suspected of using AI for lectures—Yingling frames AI adoption not as cheating but as a spiritual problem: the willing forfeit of the inner life for the convenience of an external voice. He surveys university administrative responses (Harvard, Yale, Columbia, Princeton all investing in AI integration) and finds them to be Pravda-like propaganda, disconnected from what is actually happening on the ground. His central argument is that AI in the classroom homogenizes, centralizes, and ultimately destroys the irreplaceable human relationship at the core of education. He closes by arguing that, short of the university's complete collapse, institutions should take a harder line on AI integration and cheating to preserve at least the equilibrium between professionalization and genuine intellectual formation.
points: Document the actual scope of AI substitution—not just cheating but email composition, gym routines, text messages, lecture writing—before proposing any institutional response.

Resist 'AI in the classroom' initiatives from administration: the stated benefits (democratizing education, innovation) are inconsistent with what elite institutions claim to offer; the real effect is homogenization.

Understand the ceiling effect: at elite schools, the pressure students face comes from peers, parents, and the job market, not from the institution—reforms must target those forces, not just formal policy.
Recognize that standardization of teaching has already depleted the eccentric, demanding teacher type; AI integration accelerates that extinction.
Administrators considering harder enforcement should note: paradoxically, reducing the severity of punishments for cheating may do more to curb the most flagrant AI use than increasing them.
quotes: The prevalence of AI use on college campuses, particularly at 'elite' universities, is a cancer on our culture that threatens to turn a generation of promising young Americans into a class of drooling morons, and it will grotesquely disfigure, if not destroy, the university as an institute in every way that it is imagined.

Every anecdote I hear about AI use shows that there is no 'integration' happening, there is simply substitution: for learning, teaching, and conversing. These are the bare activities required to enact whatever concept of the university you would like, whether it tends towards monastery or marketplace.
A mind that no longer thinks for itself does not gain anything in the trade. It simply stops being a mind.
The best universities preach the efficiency, convenience, and countless other benefits of chaining one's intellect to a very charming machine.
There is an impassable chasm [between what schools tell donors and] the story on the ground.
